text: Gerhard Heinrich Friedrich Otto Julius Herzberg, PC CC FRSC FRS, born on December 25, 1904, in Hamburg, Germany, to Albin H. Herzberg and Ella Biber, was a German-Canadian physicist and physical chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1971 "for his contributions to the knowledge of electronic structure and geometry of molecules, particularly free radicals." He is renowned for his work in atomic and molecular spectroscopy, using these techniques to determine the structures of diatomic and polyatomic molecules, including free radicals, and for the chemical analysis of astronomical objects. Herzberg served as Chancellor of Carleton University in Ottawa from 1973 to 1980. He had an older brother, Walter, born in January 1904, and his family was atheist, a fact they kept hidden. His father died in 1914 at age 43 due to dropsy and complications from a prior heart condition. Herzberg attended Vorschule (pre-school) late after contracting measles and graduated shortly after his father's death. He married Luise Herzberg (née Oettinger), a spectroscopist and fellow researcher, in 1929; Luise died in 1971. In 1933, the Nazi Party enacted a law banning men with Jewish wives from teaching at universities; as Luise was Jewish, Herzberg and his wife began planning to leave Germany. With help from John Spinks, a visiting physical chemist from the University of Saskatchewan, Herzberg secured a position at the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon. When they left Germany in 1935, the Nazis allowed them to take only the equivalent of $2.50 each and personal belongings. Initially considering a career in astronomy, Herzberg was rejected by the Hamburg Observatory due to lack of private financial support. After completing high school at the Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums, he studied at Darmstadt University of Technology with a private scholarship and earned his Dr.-Ing. degree under Hans Rau in 1928. His most significant recognition was the 1971 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, during which he was described as "generally considered to be the world's foremost molecular spectroscopist." Herzberg received numerous honors, including being elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1951, winning the Frederic Ives Medal from the OSA in 1964, and being named an Honorary Member of the Society. The NSERC Gerhard Herzberg Canada Gold Medal for Science and Engineering, Canada's highest research award, was established in his honor in 2000. The Canadian Association of Physicists also has an annual award named after him, and the Herzberg Institute of Astrophysics is named for him. An asteroid, 3316 Herzberg, bears his name. At Carleton University, Herzberg Laboratories, belonging to the Physics and Mathematics/Statistics Departments, is named after him. The main building of John Abbott College in Montreal and a public park in Saskatoon's College Park neighborhood are also named after him. Herzberg authored influential works, including Atomic Spectra and Atomic Structure and the four-volume encyclopedic series Molecular Spectra and Molecular Structure, often referred to as the spectroscopist's bible. The first three volumes were re-issued by Krieger in 1989 with extensive new footnotes by Herzberg, and Volume IV, "Constants of diatomic molecules," is a reference work compiling known spectroscopic constants of diatomic molecules up to 1978. Gerhard Herzberg fonds are held at Library and Archives Canada and the National Research Council Canada.
